styles.history: A proportional cursive of the six pens, prominent in monumental and manuscript display.
styles.characteristics: Tall uprights, broad curves and deliberate overlaps.
styles.readability: Overlapping words may obscure reading order.
styles.verification_scope: Unvocalized font-based display typography. PNG, outlined SVG and embedded-font PDF. Combining marks refused; no historical-composition or expert authenticity verification.
styles.limitations: Unvocalized font-based Thuluth approximation. Original fsType=8 permits editable embedding; no GPOS, so combining marks are refused. Not a historical or custom stacked composition.

styles.history: A proportional book hand used widely in Arabic manuscript and modern text typography.
styles.characteristics: Rounded forms and a relatively steady baseline.
styles.readability: Dense marks require generous line spacing.
styles.verification_scope: Local Unicode corpus, glyph coverage, atomic exports, bounds, embedded fonts and visual fixtures. Reader-independent PDF extraction excluded and release-blocking.

styles.history: A compact everyday hand associated with Ottoman writing practice; distinct from classical Riqa.
styles.characteristics: Compressed forms and short strokes.
styles.readability: Handwritten simplifications cannot be inferred from Unicode alone.

styles.history: A broad historical family of angular scripts, not a single fixed alphabet.
styles.characteristics: Angular construction and strong horizontal rhythm.
styles.readability: Modern Kufi fonts do not reproduce all early manuscript forms.
styles.verification_scope: Local Unicode corpus, glyph coverage, atomic exports, bounds, embedded fonts and visual fixtures. Reader-independent PDF extraction excluded and release-blocking.
styles.implementation_label: Modern Kufi typography (Noto Kufi Arabic); not Square Kufic

styles.history: A geometric tradition associated with architectural inscriptions.
styles.characteristics: Orthogonal strokes and modular spacing.
styles.readability: A grid can conceal spelling and letter distinctions.

styles.history: A label for angular manuscript hands associated with eastern Islamic regions.
styles.characteristics: Contrasting tall ascenders and angular or tapered shapes.
styles.readability: The label encompasses substantial variation.

styles.history: An Ottoman chancery writing tradition.
styles.characteristics: Rounded sweeping forms and compact connections.
styles.readability: Compact joins can reduce readability.
styles.verification_scope: Unvocalized font-based display lettering only. PDF and combining marks are refused; no expert authenticity review.
styles.limitations: Original fsType=2 retained: PDF embedding refused. No GPOS: combining marks refused. Font-based approximate Diwani, not composed/Jali calligraphy.

styles.history: An elaborate display development of Diwani.
styles.characteristics: Dense interweaving and ornamental marks.
styles.readability: Ornamental filling is not extra linguistic text.

styles.history: A Persianate tradition especially associated with poetry and later Urdu typography.
styles.characteristics: Suspended diagonal groups and descending words.
styles.readability: Deep descenders need extra vertical room.
styles.verification_scope: Local Unicode corpus, glyph coverage, atomic exports, bounds, embedded fonts and visual fixtures. Reader-independent PDF extraction excluded and release-blocking.

styles.history: A broken cursive family, often referring to Shikasteh Nastaliq; distinguish Shikasteh Taliq.
styles.characteristics: Compressed flowing groups and less familiar connections.
styles.readability: Highly cursive writing is difficult for untrained readers.

styles.history: A Persian chancery tradition; Ottoman usage of talik can also refer to Nastaliq.
styles.characteristics: Hanging groups and fluid movement.
styles.readability: Terminology must be tied to region and period.

styles.history: A regional family of western Islamic manuscript hands.
styles.characteristics: Broad rounded bowls and regionally distinctive letter details.
styles.readability: Dot placement conventions may differ from modern eastern usage.

styles.history: A regional tradition related to the broader Maghrebi family.
styles.characteristics: Rounded forms with local manuscript variation.
styles.readability: Avoid treating it as one universal modern font style.

styles.history: One of the six proportional pens used in formal manuscript production.
styles.characteristics: Expansive letters with assertive uprights and extended strokes.
styles.readability: Needs generous horizontal space.

styles.history: A smaller, delicate hand related to Muhaqqaq within the six pens.
styles.characteristics: Fine treatment and measured forms.
styles.readability: Scaling down a Muhaqqaq font does not establish Rayhani.

styles.history: A proportional hand in the six pens with documentary associations.
styles.characteristics: Compact, rounded writing with characteristic connections.
styles.readability: Do not confuse it with a generic modern signature font.

styles.history: A classical proportional hand related to Tawqi; distinct from modern Ruqah.
styles.characteristics: Small-scale compact forms.
styles.readability: Similar transliterations cause frequent misidentification.

styles.history: A certificate-associated calligraphic tradition often discussed in relation to Naskh and Thuluth.
styles.characteristics: Combination of compact text and more expressive letter movement.
styles.readability: A certificate rendered in Naskh is not thereby Ijazah.

styles.history: A specialized Ottoman-associated style; detailed historical attribution remains under research.
styles.characteristics: See the linked attributed signature specimen; no numerical model is asserted here.
styles.readability: Evidence is limited; avoid invented rules or dates.

styles.history: An Ottoman emblem and composition tradition rather than an independent alphabet.
styles.characteristics: Intertwined names, vertical shafts and sweeping loops.
styles.readability: Emblem recognition may matter more than straightforward reading.
